full_judgment:
These two rules, at the instance of the pre-emptor-petitioners, arise out of proceedings under section 24 of the Nonagricultural Tenancy Act 1949 and are directed against concurrent judgment and order of the courts below disallowing, pre-emption. 

 4. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioners that the courts below were wrong in holding that the proceedings were bad for defect of parties. Admittedly, the transferer and the transferees in the respective cases were made parties. There is no provision under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, unlike section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, to make other co-sharer tenants of the holding party to the proceeding. In this connection the learned Advocate has referred to the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Shafique Mia vs. Meherunnessa & another (C.P.S.L.A. No. 10 of 1974) reported in the Bangladesh Supreme Court Digest Vol. 1 (1972-77) at page 236 wherein it was held that in a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act apart from the transferee anyone else need not be impleaded in the application for pre-emption. In that case while considering the question of defect of party it appears to have been held that non-joinder of widows could net defect the claim for pre-emption. In the instant case the defect of party is said to be by reason of non-joinder of the daughters of one Bashrat Ali, a co sharer of the holding. Regard being had to the aforesaid principle laid down by the Appellate Division it must be held that the instant cases could not be said to be bad for defect of parties. 

 6. In the facts and circumstances, the cases are to be sent on remand to the court of appeal below for determination of the improvement costs, if any. As to the finding of the learned Munsif that the petitioners were not non-agricultural tenants, Nothing was said by the court of appeal below. The applications under section 24 of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act are, however, clearly maintainable, inasmuch as, the learned Advocate for the purchaser-opposite parties himself concedes that the lands in dispute are non-agricultural lands being situate with-in the Feni Pourashava. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties, however, submits that the question of maintainability of the applications should be kept open to be decided by the court of appeal below in view of section .85(2) of the aforesaid Act. He has referred to a decision reported in 33 DLR loin support of his submission that the aforesaid provision stands as a bar to a proceeding under section 24 of the said Act. I have considered the facts of that case. It may be pointed out that the facts of that case are clearly distinguishable from that of the instant cases and as such what was held in that case does not at all held good in the instant cases. It is not the case here that the tenants are holding the non-agricultural land under the Government since prior to the enforcement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It was noticed in that case that in the town of Sylhet all lands were rent free wader the. Government and there was no private superior landlord as in other parts of the country. In the instant cases the right available to a non-agricultural ten-ant is protected by the proviso to section 85(2). Moreover, it was never raised in the present cases, as already observed, that the tenants were holding the disputed land under the Government since before the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, it comes to this that the petitioners are entitled to the right of pre-emption subject to the determination of the improvement costs, if any, to be decided by the lower appellate court on the basis of the evidence on record.
